- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

35-The recommended way to upgrade an existing Vite+ project is `vp migrate`:
36-
37-```bash
38-vp migrate
39-```
40-
41:On a project that is already on Vite+, migrate does a toolchain version upgrade only: it re-pins `vite-plus`, the `vite` -> `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core` alias, and the `vitest` pin to the versions the global `vp` now bundles, across every workspace package. It skips the first-time setup steps (git hooks, editor and agent files, lint migration), so a version bump does not re-touch things you already configured. Pass `--full` to also run that setup.
42-
43-### Updating the Vitest Pin
44-
45-If you migrated with `vp migrate`, your project pins `vitest` to an exact version so the whole project shares a single Vitest copy with the bundled `vp test` runner. The pin lives in your package manager's override block:
46-
47-- **npm / Bun:** a `vitest` entry under `overrides` in `package.json`
48-- **Yarn:** a `vitest` entry under `resolutions` in `package.json`
49-- **pnpm:** a `vitest` entry under `overrides` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` — unless your `package.json` already had a `pnpm` field, in which case it lives under `pnpm.overrides` in `package.json` instead (pnpm ignores `pnpm-workspace.yaml` overrides when `package.json` defines `pnpm.overrides`)
50-
51-A Vite+ release can bump the bundled Vitest. Because that pin also applies to `vite-plus`'s own `vitest` dependency, an out-of-date pin keeps installing the previous runner even after you upgrade `vite-plus` — splitting Vitest's internals (mocks, `expect`, runner state) between the pinned copy and the one `vp test` loads.
52-
53-After upgrading `vite-plus`, re-pin `vitest` to the version Vite+ now bundles. Check that version with:
54-
55-```bash
56-vp --version
57-```
58-
59-Then set the `vitest` override to that exact version, or rerun `vp migrate` to update the pin for you.
60-
61-## Preview Builds
62-
63-Some Vite+ pull requests publish temporary packages for testing before an npm release. Treat these as nightly or bleeding-edge builds: they are useful when you want to verify a specific fix, test a fresh upstream dependency bump, or confirm a change before the next release. For day-to-day work, prefer the published `latest` release.
64-
65-Each commit on an eligible pull request is published to the [registry bridge](https://registry-bridge.viteplus.dev/). The bridge serves these builds as ordinary npm versions of the form `0.0.0-commit.<sha>` and proxies every other package to the npm registry. That means you install a preview with normal version specs instead of mutable URLs, and the same versions resolve in CI.
66-
67:Both `vite-plus` and `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core` publish under the same `0.0.0-commit.<sha>` version. Each pull request carries a comment listing the exact version for its latest commit, along with ready-to-copy install steps.
68-
69-You can find preview builds in pull requests that automatically update upstream dependencies. For examples, search the merged pull requests for [upstream dependency updates](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/vite-plus/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+upgrade+upstream+dependencies).
70-
71-Preview builds are addressed by pull request number or commit SHA. They are not a stable version range, and you should avoid leaving them in long-lived branches unless a maintainer asks you to.
72-
73-### Global `vp` Preview
74-
75-Install a preview build of the global CLI by passing `VP_PR_VERSION` to the installer. Pass a pull request number or a commit SHA:
76-
77-```bash
78-curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | VP_PR_VERSION=<pr-or-sha> bash
79-```
80-
81-On Windows:
82-
83-```powershell
84-$env:VP_PR_VERSION = "<pr-or-sha>"
85-irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex
86-Remove-Item Env:\VP_PR_VERSION
87-```
--
93-After installing the preview global CLI above, run migrate in the project to move its local `vite-plus` onto the same build:
94-
95-```bash
96-vp migrate
97-```
98-
99:Migrate points the project at the bridge registry (writing it to `.npmrc`, or `.yarnrc.yml` for Yarn Berry) and pins `vite-plus` and the `vite` -> `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core` alias to the matching `0.0.0-commit.<sha>` version. That registry line is what lets the same versions resolve in the project's own CI, so commit it if you want CI to test the preview too.
100-
101-After installing, check the bundled versions with `vp --version`. When testing is complete, restore the published release: set `vite-plus` back to `latest`, remove the bridge `registry` line from `.npmrc` (or `.yarnrc.yml`), and reinstall with `vp install`.

**Fixed.** `vp install`, `vp check` (52 files formatted, 0 lint/type errors), and `vp test` (17 tests, 4 files) all pass. One-line change:

```diff
   "overrides": {
-    "vite": "npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.5"
+    "vite": "npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.8"
   }
```

## On removing the override

I tested it rather than guessing. Short answer: not while you're on Vite+ with npm, and there's no version on the horizon that changes that.

**Removing it entirely** — npm installs upstream `vite@8.2.1` at `node_modules/vite`. You'd then have two Vites: the real one that plugins import, and `vite-plus-core@0.2.8` that `vp dev`/`vp build` actually runs.

**Replacing it with a plain aliased devDependency** (`"vite": "npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.8"`, no `overrides` block) — npm refuses to install at all:

```
npm error Found: vite@0.2.8
npm error Could not resolve dependency:
npm error peer vite@"^5.2.0 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8" from @tailwindcss/vite@4.3.3
```

The alias resolves as version **0.2.8**, which satisfies nobody's `^8` peer range. Eleven packages in your tree declare a `vite` peer — `@tailwindcss/vite`, `@vitejs/plugin-react`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/router-plugin`, `@rolldown/plugin-babel`, `nitro`, `vitest`, and others. `overrides` is the only npm mechanism that bypasses peer-range checking, which is precisely why Vite+ uses it.

It goes away when those third-party plugins import `vite-plus` instead of bare `vite` — the `vp migrate` help hints at this ("Confirm `vite` imports were rewritten to `vite-plus` where needed"), but that's an ecosystem-wide change, not a Vite+ release.

## What you can drop is the hand-maintenance

`vp migrate` (no `--full`) re-pins `vite-plus` **and** the alias together across all workspace packages. That's exactly the drift that broke this — the last "Updated dependencies" commit bumped `vite-plus` 0.2.7 → 0.2.8 but left the override at 0.2.5. Using `vp migrate` for toolchain bumps instead of editing `package.json` by hand prevents a repeat. I didn't run it since it rewrites `package.json` and possibly `.npmrc` — your call.

Two notes:

- The Vite+ docs also describe a `vitest` pin in `overrides`, which you don't have. Currently harmless — I checked, there's exactly one `vitest@4.1.10` and zero nested copies, because your exact devDependency pin happens to match what `vite-plus` depends on. Same class of drift risk if a future release bumps the bundled Vitest, but nothing to do today.
- **This is uncommitted.** CI running `npm ci` against the committed lock will still resolve core 0.2.5 and fail identically. `package.json` and `package-lock.json` both need to go in. (`bun.lock` also shows as deleted — separate pre-existing change, I left it alone.)

# Continuous Integration

You can use `voidzero-dev/setup-vp` to use Vite+ in CI environments.

## Overview

[`voidzero-dev/setup-vp`](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/setup-vp) provides integrations for GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD. Both install Vite+ and can install project dependencies. The GitHub Action can also set up Node.js and cache package manager data automatically, while the GitLab CI/CD template uses the Node.js runtime and cache configuration provided by the job.

## GitHub Actions

The GitHub Action sets up Vite+, the required Node.js version, and the package manager. This means you usually do not need separate `setup-node`, package-manager setup, or manual dependency caching steps in your workflow.

```yaml [.github/workflows/ci.yml]
- uses: voidzero-dev/setup-vp@v1
  with:
    node-version: '24'
    cache: true
- run: vp install
- run: vp check
- run: vp test
- run: vp build
```

With `cache: true`, `setup-vp` handles dependency caching for you automatically.

::: tip
`setup-vp` caches package-manager data. To reuse Vite Task results across CI runs, add a separate [GitHub Actions cache for Vite Task](/guide/github-actions-cache).
:::

## GitLab CI/CD

Use the reusable `setup-vp` remote template in your GitLab CI/CD configuration:

```yaml [.gitlab-ci.yml]
include:
  - remote: 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/voidzero-dev/setup-vp/v1/gitlab/setup-vp.yml'

test:
  extends: .setup-vp
  image: node:24
  script:
    - vp check
    - vp test
    - vp build
```

The GitLab CI/CD integration differs from the GitHub Action in a few ways:

- The template does not install Node.js. Use a Node.js image, as shown above, or otherwise provide Node.js in the job.
- Configure dependency caching with the job's GitLab [`cache`](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/#cache) keyword.
- Use a Unix-like runner environment with Bash and either `curl` or `wget`.

For advanced configuration and the complete input reference, see the [`setup-vp` GitLab CI/CD documentation](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/setup-vp#gitlab-cicd).

## Simplifying Existing Workflows

If you are migrating an existing GitHub Actions workflow, you can often replace large blocks of Node, package-manager, and cache setup with a single `setup-vp` step.

#### Before:

```yaml [.github/workflows/ci.yml]
- uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
  with:
    version: 11

- uses: actions/setup-node@v6
  with:
    node-version: '24'
    cache: pnpm

- run: pnpm ci && pnpm dev:setup
- run: pnpm check
- run: pnpm test
```

#### After:

```yaml [.github/workflows/ci.yml]
- uses: voidzero-dev/setup-vp@v1
  with:
    node-version: '24'
    cache: true

- run: vp install && vp run dev:setup
- run: vp check
- run: vp test
```

1	# Troubleshooting
2	
3	Use this page when something in Vite+ is not behaving the way you expect.
4	
5	::: info
6	Vite+ is in beta: stable, but not yet complete. We are adding features on the road to 1.0 and prioritize community feedback, so please [reach out](#asking-for-help) if something does not work as expected.
7	:::
8	
9	## Supported Tool Versions
10	
11	Vite+ expects modern upstream tool versions.
12	
13	- Vite 8 or newer
14	- Vitest 4.1 or newer
15	
16	If you are migrating an existing project and it still depends on older Vite or Vitest versions, upgrade those first before adopting Vite+.
17	
18	## `vp check` does not run type-aware lint rules or type checks
19	
20	- Confirm that `lint.options.typeAware` and `lint.options.typeCheck` are enabled in `vite.config.ts`
21	- Check whether your `tsconfig.json` still uses `compilerOptions.baseUrl`
22	
23	The Oxlint type checker path powered by `tsgolint` does not support `baseUrl`.
24	`vp migrate` and `vp lint --init` try to run the `vp dlx @andrewbranch/ts5to6 --fixBaseUrl .`
25	fix before enabling type-aware linting. If that fix fails or is declined, Vite+
26	skips `typeAware` and `typeCheck`.
27	
28	## VS Code extension does not read `vite.config.ts`
29	
30	If VS Code has multiple folders open, the shared Oxc language server may pick a different workspace than expected. That can make it look like `vite.config.ts` support is missing.
31	
32	- Confirm the extension is using the intended workspace.
33	
34	## `vp dev` or `vp build` does not run my script
35	
36	Unlike package managers, built-in commands cannot be overwritten. If you are trying to run a `package.json` script use `vp run <script>` instead.
37	
38	For example:
39	
40	- `vp dev` always starts the built-in Vite dev server
41	- `vp build` always runs the built-in Vite build
42	- `vp test` always runs the built-in Vitest command
43	- `vp run dev`, `vp run build`, and `vp run test` run the matching `package.json` scripts instead
44	
45	See [Built-in Commands vs Scripts](/guide/run#built-in-commands-vs-scripts) for when to prefer each path.
46	
47	::: info
48	You can also run custom tasks defined in `vite.config.ts` and migrate away from `package.json` scripts entirely.
49	:::
50	
51	## Staged Checks and Commit Hooks
52	
53	If `vp staged` fails or your pre-commit hook does not run:
54	
55	- make sure `vite.config.ts` contains a `staged` block
56	- make sure the project-owned pre-commit hook runs `vp staged`
57	- run `vp config` to install the hook dispatcher
58	- check whether hook installation was skipped intentionally through `VP_GIT_HOOKS=0`
59	
60	A minimal staged config looks like this:
61	
62	```ts [vite.config.ts]
63	import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';
64	
65	export default defineConfig({
66	  staged: {
67	    '*': 'vp check --fix',
68	  },
69	});
70	```
71	
72	## Slow config loading caused by heavy plugins
73	
74	When `vite.config.ts` imports plugins at the top level, they are evaluated for every command, including `vp lint`, `vp fmt`, editor integrations, and long-lived background processes. This can make config loading slow and may trigger plugin setup side effects, such as reading files, starting watchers, or connecting to services.
75	
76	Use `lazyPlugins` to skip the plugin factory when vite-plus loads your config only to read a metadata block (`lint`, `fmt`, `check`, `staged`, `pack`, `create`, the `run`/`cache` task lookup, and editor tooling). The plugins still load whenever Vite actually runs, `dev`, `build`, `test`, `preview`, and any build your own scripts spawn (a `vp run` task, `vp exec`):
77	
78	```ts [vite.config.ts]
79	import { defineConfig, lazyPlugins } from 'vite-plus';
80	import myPlugin from 'vite-plugin-foo';
81	
82	export default defineConfig({
83	  plugins: lazyPlugins(() => [myPlugin()]),
84	});
85	```
86	
87	For heavy plugins that should be lazily imported, combine with dynamic `import()`:
88	
89	```ts [vite.config.ts]
90	import { defineConfig, lazyPlugins } from 'vite-plus';
91	
92	export default defineConfig({
93	  plugins: lazyPlugins(async () => {
94	    const { default: heavyPlugin } = await import('vite-plugin-heavy');
95	    return [heavyPlugin()];
96	  }),
97	});
98	```
99	
100	## Asking for Help
101	
102	If you are stuck, please reach out:
103	
104	- [Discord](https://discord.gg/cAnsqHh5PX) for real-time discussion and troubleshooting help
105	- [GitHub](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/vite-plus) for issues, discussions, and bug reports
106	
107	When reporting a problem, please include:
108	
109	- The full output of `vp env current` and `vp --version`
110	- The package manager used by the project
111	- The exact steps needed to reproduce the problem and your `vite.config.ts`
112	- A minimal reproduction repository or runnable sandbox

skips `typeAware` and `typeCheck`.

## VS Code extension does not read `vite.config.ts`

If VS Code has multiple folders open, the shared Oxc language server may pick a different workspace than expected. That can make it look like `vite.config.ts` support is missing.

- Confirm the extension is using the intended workspace.

## `vp dev` or `vp build` does not run my script

Unlike package managers, built-in commands cannot be overwritten. If you are trying to run a `package.json` script use `vp run <script>` instead.

For example:

- `vp dev` always starts the built-in Vite dev server
- `vp build` always runs the built-in Vite build
- `vp test` always runs the built-in Vitest command
- `vp run dev`, `vp run build`, and `vp run test` run the matching `package.json` scripts instead

See [Built-in Commands vs Scripts](/guide/run#built-in-commands-vs-scripts) for when to prefer each path.

::: info
You can also run custom tasks defined in `vite.config.ts` and migrate away from `package.json` scripts entirely.
:::

## Staged Checks and Commit Hooks

If `vp staged` fails or your pre-commit hook does not run:

- make sure `vite.config.ts` contains a `staged` block
- make sure the project-owned pre-commit hook runs `vp staged`
- run `vp config` to install the hook dispatcher
- check whether hook installation was skipped intentionally through `VP_GIT_HOOKS=0`

A minimal staged config looks like this:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig({
  staged: {
    '*': 'vp check --fix',
  },
});
```

## Slow config loading caused by heavy plugins

When `vite.config.ts` imports plugins at the top level, they are evaluated for every command, including `vp lint`, `vp fmt`, editor integrations, and long-lived background processes. This can make config loading slow and may trigger plugin setup side effects, such as reading files, starting watchers, or connecting to services.

Use `lazyPlugins` to skip the plugin factory when vite-plus loads your config only to read a metadata block (`lint`, `fmt`, `check`, `staged`, `pack`, `create`, the `run`/`cache` task lookup, and editor tooling). The plugins still load whenever Vite actually runs, `dev`, `build`, `test`, `preview`, and any build your own scripts spawn (a `vp run` task, `vp exec`):

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig, lazyPlugins } from 'vite-plus';
import myPlugin from 'vite-plugin-foo';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: lazyPlugins(() => [myPlugin()]),
});
```

For heavy plugins that should be lazily imported, combine with dynamic `import()`:

```ts [vite.config.ts]
import { defineConfig, lazyPlugins } from 'vite-plus';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: lazyPlugins(async () => {
    const { default: heavyPlugin } = await import('vite-plugin-heavy');
    return [heavyPlugin()];
  }),
});
```

## Asking for Help

If you are stuck, please reach out:

- [Discord](https://discord.gg/cAnsqHh5PX) for real-time discussion and troubleshooting help
- [GitHub](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/vite-plus) for issues, discussions, and bug reports

When reporting a problem, please include:

- The full output of `vp env current` and `vp --version`
- The package manager used by the project
- The exact steps needed to reproduce the problem and your `vite.config.ts`
- A minimal reproduction repository or runnable sandbox

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Vite+ migration, overrides, and vite-plus-core alias best practices for 2026:

## Package Manager Overrides

When migrating to Vite+, you need to add overrides to your package manager so that other packages resolve the Vite+ versions: alias vite to @voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core, and pin vitest to the version Vite+ bundles.

## Override Configuration Example

The recommended overrides configuration is: `"overrides": { "vite": "npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@latest", "vitest": "4.1.10" }`

## Why Overrides Matter

You need these overrides so the whole project shares a single Vitest copy with vp test. Without proper pinning, an out-of-date pin keeps installing the previous runner even after you upgrade vite-plus, splitting Vitest's internals (mocks, expect, runner state) between the pinned copy and the one vp test loads.

## Migration Best Practices

For 0.1.x to 0.2.x upgrades, do not trust vp migrate as the only step. Remove @voidzero-dev/vite-plus-test, keep only the vite -> @voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core alias, and classify any direct Vitest, coverage, UI, or browser-provider usage before deciding which upstream Vitest packages must remain direct dependencies.

On a project that is already on Vite+, migrate does a toolchain version upgrade only: it re-pins vite-plus, the vite -> @voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core alias, and the vitest pin to the versions the global vp now bundles, across every workspace package.

on:
  push:

jobs:

Research done. Two corrections to what I told you earlier, then the findings.

## Your machine is fine — and this wasn't drift going unnoticed

`vp env doctor`: all checks passed. The real cause is a deliberate breaking change in `vite-plus@0.2.8`. I checked the `./binding` subpath export across every release:

| version | `./binding` export |
|---|---|
| 0.2.5 | present |
| 0.2.6 | present |
| 0.2.7 | present |
| **0.2.8** | **removed** |

`@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.5` finds its native Rolldown binding by requiring `vite-plus/binding`. That worked against vite-plus 0.2.5–0.2.7, so your stale override was **harmless until 0.2.8**. In 0.2.8 the binding moved into per-platform packages — `core@0.2.5` declares only `fsevents` as an optional dep, while `core@0.2.8` declares all 8 platform packages. The release notes describe it as resolving the binding "through platform packages instead of an undeclared require back into vite-plus." It's an upstream fix that requires the alias to move in lockstep.

**Corrections to my earlier message:** I said the last commit bumped `vite-plus` 0.2.7 → 0.2.8 and that CI would fail on the committed lock. Both wrong. Commit `cdc2b26` has `vite-plus@0.2.7` and CI was **green** on it — correctly, since 0.2.7 still exported `./binding`. The 0.2.8 bump is uncommitted working-tree state. CI didn't miss this; it never ran on it. (The `darwin-arm64` string in your error is just your platform in the fallback chain — the `./binding` failure is platform-agnostic.)

I also verified the regenerated lock carries all 8 platform bindings at 0.2.8 including `linux-x64-gnu`, and that `vp install --frozen-lockfile` (the CI path, ubuntu-latest) succeeds. That's the one thing a passing macOS run wouldn't have told you.

## Best practices for this repo

**1. Use `vp migrate` for toolchain bumps.** It re-pins `vite-plus`, the `vite` alias, and the `vitest` pin together across all workspace packages — precisely the lockstep this failure needed. Hand-editing `package.json` is what let them diverge. Run it without `--full` so it won't re-touch hooks/editor/agent config you've already set up.

**2. Add the `vitest` entry to `overrides`.** The documented shape is both keys, not one:

```json
"overrides": {
  "vite": "npm:@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-core@0.2.8",
  "vitest": "4.1.10"
}
```

Benign today — I verified exactly one `vitest@4.1.10`, zero nested copies, because your exact devDependency pin happens to match what `vite-plus` bundles. It becomes a real problem when a release bumps the bundled Vitest and the two copies split `expect`/mocks/runner state. I haven't applied it; say the word.

**3. Env var rename — cleared.** 0.2.8 renamed three Vite+ env vars to a `VP_*` prefix with no compatibility aliases. I grepped your source, configs, workflows, Dockerfile, and `.env*` (you have none): zero usages. Nothing to do.

**4. Minor: CI could use `vp check`.** `fly.yml` runs `vp lint` and `vp run typecheck` as separate steps; the docs' example uses a single `vp check` (format + lint + typecheck, parallelized). A simplification only — **it would not have caught this failure**, so don't read it as the fix.

I did *not* attribute this to Dependabot. Your `dependabot.yml` is daily/ungrouped, but the override bumps in history are hand-authored (`8451dd6` "Bump Vite+ core to 0.2.5 and drop redundant overrides"), and Dependabot's PRs land under the `npm_and_yarn in /.` titles. Whatever updated deps in your working tree, `vp migrate` is the guard.

## And on "ideally no override"

Unchanged, and it's the hardest evidence I have. Removing `overrides` entirely installs upstream `vite@8.2.1` alongside vite-plus-core — two Vites. Replacing it with a plain aliased devDependency fails to install at all:

```
npm error Could not resolve dependency:
npm error peer vite@"^5.2.0 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8" from @tailwindcss/vite@4.3.3
```

The alias resolves as version **0.2.8**, satisfying no `^8` range. Eleven packages in your tree declare a `vite` peer. `overrides` is the only npm mechanism that bypasses peer-range checking — which is why Vite+ specifies it.

Still uncommitted: `package.json` + `package-lock.json`.

Sources: [Vite+ upgrade guide](https://viteplus.dev/guide/upgrade), [Vite+ migrate guide](https://viteplus.dev/guide/migrate), [vite-plus releases](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/vite-plus/releases), [discussion #990 on alias + overrides](https://github.com/voidzero-dev/vite-plus/discussions/990), plus the version-matched local docs in `node_modules/vite-plus/docs`.

Scaffolded both a fresh `vite:application` and `vite:library` on npm. The reference config, versus yours:

| | fresh scaffold | your repo |
|---|---|---|
| `overrides.vite` alias @ current version | ✓ | ✓ (after the fix) |
| direct `vitest` dep | **absent in both** | `4.1.10` |
| `vitest` in `overrides` | **absent in both** | absent |
| `@vitest/coverage-v8` | n/a (no coverage) | `4.1.10` |
| package manager decl | `devEngines.packageManager` + `onFail: "download"` | legacy `packageManager: "npm@11.12.1"` |

**Correction: my earlier advice to add `"vitest": "4.1.10"` to `overrides` was wrong for this repo.** Superseded — the right move is to *delete* `vitest`, not pin it. Your tests import from `vite-plus/test`, not `vitest`; a repo-wide grep found zero direct `vitest` imports. Neither template carries the dep or the override. I proved it in a copy of your project: with `vitest` removed, **17/17 tests pass with coverage**, one `vitest@4.1.10` in the tree, supplied by `vite-plus`.

`@vitest/coverage-v8` must stay — removing it fails hard with `MISSING DEPENDENCY  Cannot find dependency '@vitest/coverage-v8'`, and `fly.yml` runs exactly that command. Keep its version tracking the bundled Vitest (`vp --version` → 4.1.10). That's the one real drift risk left.

**Best incidental catch: `coverage/` is not gitignored.** CI runs `vp test run --coverage`; any local run leaves 15 untracked generated files. Worse, your `staged` hook is `"*": "vp check --fix"` — so it would try to *format generated HTML* on your next commit. I reproduced it: `vp check` flagged all 15. Two-line fix — add `coverage/` to `.gitignore` and to the `ignorePatterns` in `vite.config.ts` next to the existing `.output/**`, `dist/**`.

Two things I'm **not** recommending you change:

- The app template has the alias in `devDependencies` *and* `overrides`; the library template only in `overrides`. The overrides entry is the universal part — the devDep alias shows up only where the upstream template already had a `vite` devDep to rewrite. Yours has none and imports nothing from `vite`, so there's nothing to add.
- `devEngines.packageManager` is the modern shape and your npm pin is two majors behind the scaffold's 12.0.2 — but package-manager bumps carry their own blast radius, and you didn't ask.

Your `vite.config.ts` is otherwise ahead of the templates — `lazyPlugins` and `staged` are both things the scaffolds don't generate.

## Recommendation

One commit, three changes: the override fix (already applied), drop `vitest` from `devDependencies`, and gitignore + fmt-ignore `coverage/`. All three are verified, and the last two prevent the next papercut. Want me to apply the two remaining and commit?
